clinicalPearls: The rarest form of angiokeratoma, usually congenital or appearing in infancy or childhood and most often on a lower limb.
Presents as a unilateral, well-demarcated cluster or plaque of dark-red to blue-black hyperkeratotic vascular papules and nodules, sometimes in a linear or segmental (blaschkoid) pattern.
Represents ectatic superficial dermal vessels with overlying epidermal hyperkeratosis and acanthosis.
May slowly enlarge and can bleed after minor trauma.
Distinct from the systemic angiokeratomas of Fabry disease (angiokeratoma corporis diffusum), which are widespread and symmetrical.
Dermoscopy typically shows dark lacunae with an overlying whitish keratotic veil.
May coexist with an underlying venous or lymphatic malformation in some cases.
Treatment with laser or excision is undertaken for cosmesis or troublesome bleeding, but recurrence is possible.
reference.pathophysiology: Angiokeratoma circumscriptum is a localised vascular ectasia in which dilated, thin-walled capillaries and postcapillary venules occupy the superficial papillary dermis, closely apposed to a reactively hyperkeratotic and acanthotic epidermis that may partially enclose the ectatic vessels. Unlike the angiokeratomas of Fabry disease and other lysosomal storage disorders, it is not associated with a systemic enzyme deficiency. It behaves as a localised capillary and venous malformation, sometimes overlying a deeper vascular malformation, with the keratotic surface reflecting secondary epidermal change over long-standing dilated vessels.
additionalDifferentials: Other localised angiokeratomas (Mibelli, Fordyce and solitary types)
Malignant melanoma in a pigmented, bleeding lesion
additionalInvestigations: Dermoscopy showing dark lacunae with a keratotic veil
Skin biopsy confirming dilated superficial vessels with overlying hyperkeratosis
Ultrasound or MRI if a deeper vascular malformation is suspected
Screening for Fabry disease (alpha-galactosidase A activity) if lesions are widespread or symmetrical
Assessment of the extent of any associated malformation
redFlags: Pigmented or rapidly changing lesion raising suspicion of melanoma
Widespread symmetrical angiokeratomas suggesting a systemic storage disorder
Rapid enlargement suggesting an underlying deeper malformation
reference.prognosis: Angiokeratoma circumscriptum is benign and persists lifelong, tending to enlarge slowly. Treatment is undertaken for bleeding or cosmetic reasons, with a recognised risk of recurrence after ablative therapy.
pitfalls: Confusing localised angiokeratoma circumscriptum with the systemic angiokeratomas of Fabry disease and missing a treatable metabolic condition.
Mistaking a bleeding, keratotic and pigmented lesion for melanoma, or the reverse.
Treating superficially without recognising a deeper underlying malformation.
references: Reviews of cutaneous angiokeratomas and their differential diagnosis
management: Surgical excision for localised symptomatic or cosmetically troublesome lesions, with counselling about recurrence after ablative treatment
Vascular laser therapy such as pulsed-dye or long-pulsed Nd:YAG laser as a less invasive option for suitable lesions
Local measures to control bleeding from lesions traumatised at the surface
Imaging with ultrasound or MRI to define any deeper underlying vascular malformation before intervention
Exclude Fabry disease by measuring alpha-galactosidase A activity if lesions are widespread or symmetrical rather than localised
Reassurance regarding the benign nature and lifelong persistence, with monitoring for slow enlargement
